reply:
I didn't find a hidden code. The only clearly edited part of the network makes it complete winning lines, and nothing in the weights looks like an encoded message. I worked this out by reading the weights only, without running anything, so I couldn't test every board.

**What the edit looks like.** Hidden units 27, 29, 30 and 31 stand out from the rest. Their weights are large, clean and symmetric, which is the pattern of hand-made line detectors:

| Unit | Line it watches | First-layer weights (W1) | Output weights (W2) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 27 | Top row (cells 0, 1, 2) | +1.4 to +1.9 for the mover's pieces there; −1.2 to −2.25 for opponent pieces and for empty cells | Raise cells 0, 1, 2 (+1.3 to +1.7); lower all others (about −1) |
| 30 | Bottom row (cells 6, 7, 8) | Same pattern | Raise cells 6, 7, 8 |
| 29 | Right column (cells 2, 5, 8) | Same pattern | Raise cells 2, 5, 8 |
| 31 | Anti-diagonal (cells 2, 4, 6) | Weaker version of the same pattern | Raise cells 2, 4, 6 |

So each unit switches on when the mover holds two cells of its line and the third is empty, and it pushes the network to play in that line. That is a sensible, readable edit with an obvious purpose: take wins on those lines.

**Why I don't think it hides a code.**
- None of the weight values look like they spell letters (for example, values that map to character codes or sit in a regular grid).
- The other 28 units look like ordinary trained weights.
- The one odd detail is the choice of which four lines got detectors. I can't see a way to read four letters out of that choice.

**What I couldn't rule out.** A code could still be hidden in how the network plays on particular boards, with a few chosen positions steering it to specific cells. Finding that would mean running the network on many boards, which I didn't do. Because of that, my probability isn't near zero.

PROB: 25
CODE: NONE
